nameStory: The shining willow gets its name from its remarkably glossy leaves that catch and reflect sunlight like nature's own mirrors. When a breeze moves through a stand of these willows, the leaves shimmer and dance with an almost metallic gleam that's visible from quite a distance. It's also called 'whiplash willow' in some regions because its long, flexible branches can snap back like a whip when bent.
description: Shining willow is a large shrub or small tree that can grow anywhere from 13 to 49 feet tall, making it one of the more substantial willows you'll encounter. Its most striking feature is its exceptionally glossy, dark green leaves that shine like they've been polished. The tree has a somewhat irregular, open crown with flexible branches that sway gracefully in the wind. Like other willows, it's always found near water and produces fuzzy yellow catkins in late spring.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves 4-7 inches long with an unmistakable glossy, almost waxy shine on top - they feel smooth and slippery to the touch, while the undersides are often pale blue-green and may feel slightly fuzzy

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow catkins 1-3 inches long that appear in late spring after the leaves have emerged, giving off a subtle honey-like fragrance when you get close

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a large shrub or small tree up to 49 feet tall with an open, irregular crown and long, flexible branches that bend easily without breaking

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth gray-brown bark on older trunks with shallow furrows, while younger shoots are greenish-brown and feel smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Small, pointed buds that are reddish-brown in winter and sit close to the twig, covered by a single cap-like scale that feels slightly sticky when fresh

habitat: Look for shining willow in wetland areas throughout New England, especially along stream banks, pond edges, and in marshy areas with consistently moist soil. It thrives in full sun to partial shade and is often found growing alongside other moisture-loving trees like red maple, black ash, and other willow species. You're most likely to spot it in low-lying areas where water stands or flows regularly.

seasonality.spring: Bright yellow catkins emerge in late spring after the leaves have started to unfurl, creating a beautiful contrast against the fresh green foliage. The new leaves emerge with an especially intense glossy shine.
seasonality.summer: The tree is in full leaf with its characteristic mirror-like foliage at peak shine. Seeds develop from the catkins and are released as fluffy, cotton-like material that drifts on the wind.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to yellow-green before dropping, though the color change is often subtle. The glossy leaf surface remains apparent even as they begin to fade.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the tree's open, somewhat irregular structure. The smooth, reddish-brown buds and flexible young shoots help distinguish it from other winter trees.

funFact: Shining willow leaves are so reflective that indigenous peoples traditionally used them as natural mirrors for personal grooming and signaling, and the leaves can actually reduce the air temperature around the tree by reflecting sunlight away instead of absorbing it as heat.
confusionNotes: Shining willow is most easily confused with other large willows like black willow, but the incredibly glossy leaf surface is a dead giveaway - run your finger across a shining willow leaf and it feels almost slippery, while other willows have more matte surfaces. Remember: if it doesn't truly shine like a mirror in the sunlight, it's probably not a shining willow.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Pacific willow' in western North America, this is the exact same species as our New England shining willow - it's just one tree with many regional names. The scientific name 'lucida' literally means 'shining' in Latin, which botanists chose specifically because of those remarkably glossy leaves.
compareHints: Among New England's willows, shining willow stands out for its exceptional height and mirror-like leaves. While pussy willow is famous for its fuzzy catkins and tends to stay shrub-sized, and black willow has darker, less glossy foliage, shining willow combines impressive size with unmistakable leaf shine. Its late-spring flowering (after leaves emerge) also differs from early bloomers like pussy willow that flower before their leaves appear.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many willow species, pussy willow stands out for its exceptionally soft, silvery catkins that appear before the leaves.
Bearberry willow is instantly distinguished from all other New England willows by its unique prostrate growth - every other willow species grows upright as shrubs or trees.
Among New England's willows, heart-leaved willow stands out for its combination of thick, persistently fuzzy-bottomed leaves with heart-shaped bases.
Among New England's willows, Bebb's willow stands out for its dense thicket-forming habit and adaptability to various soil types.

Among New England willows, rusty willow is most similar to grey willow (Salix cinerea), but rusty willow's twigs have that distinctive reddish-brown coloration versus grey willow's more grayish twigs.
Among New England's many willow species, black willow stands out as the largest tree form with the darkest bark.
Among New England willows, prairie willow is unique in preferring dry, sunny sites while most others need moist to wet conditions.
Grey willow differs from native pussy willow by having much more pronounced silvery-gray, woolly leaf undersides and tends to form denser thickets.
Among New England's many willows, silky willow stands out for its distinctly silky leaf undersides - most other willows have smooth or only lightly hairy leaf backs.
Interior sandbar willow stands out from other New England willows by having the narrowest leaves in the genus - much thinner than pussy willow's oval leaves or black willow's lance-shaped ones.
Meadow willow is much shorter and more colony-forming than most other New England willows like black willow or pussy willow.
Among New England's willows, purple willow is unique for its purple-red bark and blue-green leaves - pussy willow has gray bark and broader leaves, while black willow has dark, furrowed bark.

Unlike the familiar pussy willow with its large, fuzzy catkins and broad leaves, or the water-loving black willow with its narrow leaves, tea-leafed willow has those distinctive thick, oval leaves with prominent parallel veining.
Among New England willows, sage-leaf willow is unique for its distinctly fuzzy, silvery leaves that truly resemble herb sage.
Among New England's many willows, balsam willow is unique for its strong balsam fragrance - most other willows are essentially scentless.
Among New England willows, least willow is unmistakable due to its ground-hugging growth - all other willows in our region grow as upright shrubs or trees.
Bog willow differs from its willow relatives by staying much shorter and preferring acidic bog conditions rather than streamside locations.
Among New England's many willows, satiny willow stands out for having the most dramatically silvery leaf undersides—much more pronounced than the similar silky willow or sage-leaf willow.
Among New England's willows, white willow stands out for its especially silvery leaf undersides and larger mature size.
Unlike the familiar pussy willow with its large, showy catkins and bigger leaves, or the tall black willow found along rivers, Labrador willow stays remarkably small and compact.
Unlike native New England willows such as pussy willow or black willow, dappled willow has variegated foliage and often opposite leaves rather than alternate ones.

Among New England willows, autumn willow stands out for its completely hairless leaves and stems - unlike pussy willow's fuzzy twigs, silky willow's silky leaf undersides, or meadow willow's slightly hairy stems.
Among New England's willows, blueleaf willow is distinguished by its blue-green foliage color - most other willows have bright green or silvery leaves.
Unlike other New England willows such as pussy willow or black willow that have upright or spreading branches, weeping willow is unmistakable due to its pendulous, drooping branch structure.
Among New England's willows, peachleaf willow stands out for its impressive tree size - most of our native willows like pussy willow or silky willow are shrubs or small trees.
Unlike most New England willows which have narrow, lance-shaped leaves, goat willow stands out with its broad, oval, wrinkled leaves that look more like those of a poplar or apple tree.

Basket willow stands out among New England's willows for its extremely narrow leaves and exceptionally long, straight, flexible branches - most native willows like pussy willow or black willow have broader leaves and shorter, less flexible shoots.
Among New England's many willow species, rose-gold pussy willow stands out for its ornamental catkin colors - most native willows like common pussy willow have plain silver-gray catkins.
